I'm reading through this text about Dmpk-deficient mice to pick out the key entities—things like the gene/protein name DMPK, the disease myotonic dystrophy, the mouse model, and the phenotypic terms like myopathy and fibrosis that need to be tagged.

Moving to the next sentence, "Myotonic dystrophy" is tagged Specific Disease, and its parenthetical acronym "DM" gets its own Specific Disease mention following the standard abbreviation-pair convention. Then "autosomal dominant disorder" following it reads as a Disease Class, similar to how "X-linked recessive disorder" was handled, while "DMPK" itself is a gene symbol, not a disease mention.

I'm now looking at "DM" in "role of DMPK in DM pathogenesis" — since it premodifies the non-disease noun "pathogenesis," this falls under Modifier rather than Specific Disease. Then for "Dmpk deficient (Dmpk-/-) mice," I'm weighing whether the deficiency adjective functions as a Modifier premodifying "mice," similar to how "G6PD deficient phenotype" was treated, even though this describes a knockout genotype rather than a classic human deficiency disorder.

I also realize this falls under the exclusion for experimental manipulations — "Dmpk deficient" describes a knockout genotype rather than a subject's disease state, so it shouldn't be annotated at all.

Now I'm working through "Dmpk-/- mice develop a late-onset, progressive skeletal myopathy that shares some pathological features with DM." I'm debating whether "myopathy" here counts as a generic disease-class head that gets individuated into Specific Disease because "skeletal" functions as an anatomic-locus premodifier, versus treating the whole course-descriptor-laden phrase as Disease Class since "late-onset" and "progressive" are just timing/severity qualifiers. I lean toward treating "late-onset, progressive skeletal myopathy" as Specific Disease because the anatomic qualifier "skeletal" individuates it, whereas the earlier, bare "late onset progressive myopathy" (without "skeletal") in the title sentence should be Disease Class since it lacks any anatomic, etiologic, or other qualifying anchor. I'm now moving to consider "fibre degeneration" and "fibrosis" in the description of muscle pathology in mature mice.
